stories.topic: The 400-Rupee Shirt That Paid 100 Rupees in Tax
stories.summary: Ajay follows one shirt through four stages under a 'mild' 10% tax on every sale. A farmer sells cotton for 100, a spinner sells yarn for 200, the cloth is sold to a tailor for 300, and the tailor sells the shirt for 400. Each invoice carries 10%, so the government collects 10 + 20 + 30 + 40 = 100 rupees on a shirt priced at 400, an effective 25%. He then runs the same chain as a VAT. Each seller deducts the tax already paid upstream (input tax credit), so each stage remits only 10 and the total tax on the shirt is exactly 40, a true 10%.
stories.insight: A headline tax rate can hide the real burden. What matters is whether tax piles on top of tax. The same 10% can mean 25% or 10% depending purely on the design.
stories.quote: On a 400 rupee shirt, the government got 100 rupees of tax. That's 25%.

stories.summary: In 2003, Vijay Kelkar led a committee appointed by Jaswant Singh on implementing the FRBM Act. Kelkar, Arbind Modi and Ajay concluded that India's fiscal problem could not be solved without a proper VAT. But the word 'VAT' was already taken by CENVAT, a 'central VAT' that wasn't really a VAT: it didn't handle input tax credit or services correctly. To avoid confusion, they coined a new name, 'Goods and Services Tax'.
stories.insight: The GST began as a fix for India's fiscal problem, not a tax-collection scheme. Its name was a deliberate move to separate a clean idea from a flawed one that already carried the label.
stories.quote: So we coined the phrase goods and services tax as a way to just distinguish to make sure there's no confusion that no, it's not that VAT, because otherwise we'd have to explain the twenty ways in which that was not quite a VAT.

stories.topic: The Long Road From the 2003 Report to a Flawed GST
stories.summary: The authors proposed a way forward that did not need all states on board: the Centre could build an integrated tax on goods and services for itself, and states could join later. In 2004, Finance Minister Chidambaram chose not to pursue it. He cited a lack of support from state governments, and the BJP refused to take part in tax reform. The idea sat idle through ten years of Congress rule. Arun Jaitley revived it after 2014, it was announced in 2016, and it launched in 2017. By then it broke all three principles of a good VAT: many high rates and cesses, and whole sectors left out (electricity, petroleum, real estate). Input tax credit has since been increasingly blocked.
stories.insight: A good idea can be adopted in name and still lose its core. Political economy can shrink a reform until little more than the label survives.
stories.quote: So all the three principles of a good VAT were violated in the GST as it unfolded, as it came out the front door.

stories.topic: Demonetization vs GST, and a Prediction That Came True
stories.summary: In the early days of The Seen and the Unseen, Amit did short episodes on one policy at a time, including demonetization and the GST. He judged demonetization wrong in concept and in every other way. The GST, by contrast, was great in concept and terrible in implementation. His first GST guest, Devangshu Datta, predicted everything that would go wrong before the GST was even announced. A later episode with Shruti Rajagopalan covered it in full.
stories.insight: It helps to separate a policy's concept from its execution. A sound idea can still be ruined in the doing, and informed observers can often see the failures coming.
stories.quote: demonetization was just a disastrous policy measure conceptually wrong, everything was bad about it. But GST was conceptually great, but the implementation was terrible.

recommendations.item: To GST or not to GST
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar, Arbind Modi and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The Business Standard column that triggered the episode; linked in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it brilliant and incredibly insightful. It sets out the many ways the GST can still be improved, and Ajay leans on its legal analysis of how input tax credit has been blocked as the starting point for any fix.

recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar, Arbind Modi and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The early-2000s committee report, which Amit calls a seminal paper, where the GST was first proposed for India; linked in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: It is the origin of India's GST. Ajay says the right fix today is exactly what it proposed: a single low rate, a comprehensive base and no blockage of input tax credit.

recommendations.context: Amit points new viewers to it to explain why the show keeps coming back to economic growth.
recommendations.reason: It sets out the evidence that every human welfare indicator depends on rising per capita GDP, and that growth is the only way out of poverty.

recommendations.context: Ajay cites it while arguing that better GST policy needs an ecosystem of ideas outside government.
recommendations.reason: It sets out the hosts' theory of change: real policy progress comes from ideas, papers, books and public debate that shape what policymakers later do.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma

recommendations.reason: Amit describes it as a comprehensive treatment of the GST.

core_ideas.concept: Three Engines of High-Productivity Firms, and the Tax System's Duty to Stay Out of Their Way
core_ideas.explanation: Growth comes from high-productivity firms, which rest on three pillars. The first is specialization (Adam Smith's pin idea). The second is learning by doing: Wright's Law and cost experience curves say your lifetime output determines your cost efficiency. The third is globalization: removing barriers to capital, labour, goods, services and enterprise. A good tax system is neutral to all three and never tilts firms away from them.
core_ideas.quote: So the job of the tax system is never ever mess with these three. Do not come in the way.

core_ideas.explanation: Taxing 15 on a GDP of 200 is far better than taxing 15 on a GDP of 100, even though the tax-GDP ratio is lower. Many tax experts and development economists instinctively prefer the higher ratio, which confuses the means with the end. Amit links this to a mindset that treats the state as ruler rather than servant. That mindset presumes citizens guilty until proven innocent, for example by blocking input tax credit until a firm proves it is owed.
core_ideas.quote: Tax policy doesn't exist to serve the state. Tax policy exists to serve the people, i.e., to be compatible with a higher GDP.

core_ideas.concept: A Small State Can Do the Essential Job
core_ideas.explanation: The state's core tasks are peace, easy taxes, a tolerable administration of justice and a few basics, and these don't need much money. Ajay thinks the Indian state is oversized: it should tax and spend less. He also doubts it spends well; India would probably be better off if it had half the money it has today.
core_ideas.quote: In about 10% of GDP, you can become the UK of 1910.

core_ideas.concept: Bad Taxes: Why Cascading Taxes Are a Monster
core_ideas.explanation: Among economists, 'bad tax' is not a mild phrase. A tax on production at every stage taxes tax on tax, so a mild-looking rate becomes a large real burden. It attacks specialization by rewarding giant vertically integrated firms that run from petrochemicals to fabric. It hurts exporters competing with countries that have clean VATs. And it makes imports look cheap, which leads domestic firms to lobby for tariffs.
core_ideas.quote: bad taxes are mind-blowingly stupid things that only an idiot would ever do.

core_ideas.concept: The VAT and the Travel of Input Tax Credit
core_ideas.explanation: Invented by French economist Maurice Lauré in 1954, the VAT taxes only the value added at each stage. Each firm deducts the tax already paid upstream (input tax credit, or ITC), so the total tax is the same however production is split up. That makes it neutral to specialization. The flow of ITC is what makes it a VAT; without it, you are back to a production tax.
core_ideas.quote: The travel of input tax credit is the engine, is the heart of the VAT.

core_ideas.explanation: Exports carry no domestic VAT, and exporters get a refund of all their accumulated input tax credit. Goods therefore compete on world markets at tax-free prices, whatever each country's VAT rate. They then pay the importing country's VAT at its border, just as local goods do. This gives full neutrality between imports and domestic production and makes the VAT compatible with globalization.
core_ideas.quote: Good taxation is not populistic. So good taxation is done with a clean head and it is not done with emotional considerations. You do not tax foreigners. Don't bring nationalism into this.

core_ideas.concept: Low Rate, Single Rate, Comprehensive Base
core_ideas.explanation: A good VAT has a low rate (Ajay prefers 8%, at most 9% for India), no exemptions, and one rate for everything. A broad base is the path to a low rate, because a narrow base makes the ever-thirsty government push the rate up. Multiple rates invite lobbying, corruption and classification fights, such as paratha at 18% versus roti at 5%. They also overload a low-capability state. High rates encourage evasion, because economic distortion rises roughly with the square of the tax rate: doubling the rate quadruples the damage.
core_ideas.quote: The distortion imposed upon an economy goes up roughly in proportion to the tax rate squared.

core_ideas.concept: Blocked ITC: How India Partly Lost Its VAT
core_ideas.explanation: India's biggest GST failure is the growing blockage of input tax credit. Final-stage goods producers are not given proper credit on services and capital goods, and services firms face blockages too. Several 5% rates come with ITC blocked, so the real burden is far higher than the headline rate. Even delayed credit is a tax, because firms pay interest on the working capital the government holds. Across a large part of the economy, the GST has slid back into old-style excise and service tax. That disadvantages Indian producers against imports and denies exporters zero-rating.
core_ideas.quote: If you don't have correct handling of input tax credit, then it's not a VAT. Then you're back to production tax, you're back to cascading taxes.

core_ideas.concept: Tax Policy Should Be Designed by Economists, Not Tax Collectors
core_ideas.explanation: In advanced countries, economists design tax policy and administrators implement it. In Indian terms, the Department of Economic Affairs should write the law and the Department of Revenue should administer it. In India, power has shifted to the Department of Revenue. Practical officials charged with raising money now decide to block ITC for a little extra revenue, without counting the cost to GDP.
core_ideas.quote: There are meetings where a decision is being made that will block the input tax credit for this, so that we'll get a little more money. And there is nobody in that room standing there to say, but, but, but what about GDP?

core_ideas.explanation: Lasting reform comes from the climate of opinion: ideas, papers, books, blogs, seminars and public debate. Civil servants are busy firefighting, and the consultants they hire implement requests rather than supply principles. Without a strong ecosystem of ideas outside government, policy drifts away from first principles. Amit sums it up by saying policy, like politics, is downstream of culture.
core_ideas.quote: And actually all the progress in India only happens upstream of the policy maker.

core_ideas.concept: The Fix Is the Original Prescription
core_ideas.explanation: The first step, and the most urgent, is to remove every blockage of input tax credit and restore seamless end-to-end credit. After that comes a single low rate on a comprehensive base that brings every sector into the GST. Twenty years on, the cure is unchanged.
core_ideas.quote: So the answer is exactly where we were in 2003. Have a single rate, have a low rate, with a comprehensive base, and I'm embarrassed to say with no blockages against input tax credit.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit on the Business Standard column, which he admits he didn't read in print because he doesn't subscribe to any paper: policymakers across the country 'squealed in delight, unless they were part of government, where they squealed in embarrassment because all their follies were revealed to the world.'

Ajay on the 'easy' recipe for growth: 'You just have to get NVIDIA and Google emerge out of the Indian soil.' After listing the three pillars, he adds: 'It's very easy, yeah. You should try it one of these days.'
After Ajay explains that economists divide taxes into good and bad, Amit says: 'I feel like starting a hashtag not all taxes.'
On the vertically integrated petrochemicals-to-fabric giant that cascading taxes reward: 'And I have a suggested brand name for that cloth. It's called Vimal.'
Ajay: 'Every God fearing economist should stand up and put up a dharna.' Amit: 'Our economists don't fear God. They fear government. Government fearing economists should be the new term.'

Ajay's running gag about the neighbour that got its tax system right: 'a country with brilliant Bengali economists who have constructed a superior tax system? It's called Bangladesh... Because Bangladesh has only Bengali economists.'
On a low 5% GST rate that comes with blocked input tax credit: 'the taxman giveth and the taxman taketh away.'
Explaining the destination VAT: 'you know the French are very socialist, so they have a 20% VAT.'

Listing where real change comes from (ideas, papers, books, blog articles), Ajay adds: 'and you know what? It is in certain remarkable YouTube channels.' Amit later says the episode was 'edge of the seat indeed, and thankfully I haven't fallen off my chair yet.'

Maurice Lauré, the French economist who invented the VAT in 1954. Ajay uses him to rebut the idea of economics as a 'dismal science' or 'the boring game of sitting in an office and writing R programs.'

Adam Smith's pin example (specialization), Wright's Law and cost experience curves, and the show's Moore's Law episode, invoked as the foundations of firm productivity. Ajay also borrows Amit's phrase 'put in volume': 'If you've made 10,000 pins, you ain't seen nothing yet.'
The GST classification disputes: Amit's 'is KitKat a chocolate or a biscuit?' and Ajay's paratha taxed at 18% versus roti at 5%, as examples of the mess multiple rates create.
Lant Pritchett's work on development economics, cited for the evidence that every welfare indicator depends on rising per capita GDP.
The UK of 1910, an empire that ruled the world on about 10% of GDP, used to argue that the Indian state is oversized.
PricewaterhouseCoopers as shorthand for consultants who implement rather than think: 'a Price Waterhouse is not going to give them economic principles... You want to get X done, we'll get X done.'
